prompt: In `go tool pprof -top`, what does a function's `cum` column count?
hint: Compare it with `flat` on the row of `strings.Fields`.

choices.text: Samples in which it was anywhere on the stack
choices.why: Right. Its own code and everything it called, which is why `strings.Fields` had 1.20 s flat and 2.53 s cum.

choices.text: The number of times it was called during the profile
choices.why: A CPU profile counts no calls at all; `cum` is time, in samples of 10 ms.

choices.text: Samples in which it was the function running at the top of the stack
choices.why: That is `flat`. `cum` adds the samples spent in the functions it called.

choices.text: The running total of the column to its left, down the list
choices.why: That is `sum%`, which adds up `flat%` row by row.

prompt: `tally.Count` shows 0.22 s flat and 4.95 s cum, 82.50%. A colleague proposes rewriting `Count`'s own loop to make the program faster. What is the most the rewrite of that loop alone can save?
hint: Which column is the function's own code?

choices.text: Half of the cum, because flat and cum are split evenly
choices.why: There is no such split; the two columns are independent measurements.

choices.text: About 82% of the time, since `Count` is on 82.50% of the stacks
choices.why: That time is mostly spent in the functions `Count` calls; its own instructions account for the flat column only.

choices.text: About 3.7%, its flat
choices.why: Right. A delegating function's own code is its flat; the big savings are in what it calls, or how often.

choices.text: Nothing: a function with any cum cannot be optimised
choices.why: Its own 0.22 s is real time; it is just small next to what it delegates.

prompt: `strings.Fields` was on the stack for 2.53 s during 200 iterations over 100,000 lines, one call per line. About how many nanoseconds did one call cost?
hint: 2.53 s divided by 20 million calls.

prompt: With `-sample_index=alloc_objects`, `strings.Fields` and `Scanner.Text` were level at about 20 million allocations each; with `alloc_space`, `Fields` had 1,552.12 MB against 997.55 MB. What explains the difference?
hint: Same number of calls, different things allocated.

choices.text: `Text` frees its memory at once, so its bytes are not counted
choices.why: `alloc_space` counts every byte allocated, freed or not; that is what distinguishes it from `inuse_space`.

choices.text: `Fields` is called twice per line
choices.why: The equal object counts say the opposite: one call each per line.

choices.text: The sampler picked `Fields` more often by chance
choices.why: Chance explains the few percent between the counts; it cannot make one allocator's bytes half as large again as the other's.

choices.text: Both allocate once per line, but a five-string slice is bigger than a line
choices.why: Right. 5 × 16 = 80 bytes for the slice headers, against a copy of the line of about 45 bytes rounded to 48 or 64.

prompt: Which `go tool pprof` option prints a function's source with flat and cum beside every line?
hint: Section 03 used it on `tally.Parse`.

choices.text: `-peek`
choices.why: `-peek` shows callers and callees with their times, not the source lines.

choices.text: `-list`
choices.why: Right. `-list "tally.Parse"` put 2.53 s on line 27, the `strings.Fields` call.

choices.text: `-traces`
choices.why: `-traces` prints every distinct stack with its time; it does not open source files.

choices.text: `-focus`
choices.why: `-focus` filters samples by a function on the stack; the report it filters is still a list of functions.

prompt: With `-ignore=runtime`, `tally.Count` dropped from 82.50% to 37.67%. Why?
hint: What does `-ignore` do to a sample?

choices.text: Samples touching the runtime were discarded
choices.why: Right. Allocation, write barriers and preemption all happen inside `Count`'s calls, so their samples left with them.

choices.text: `Count` is itself in the runtime package
choices.why: `Count` is in `example.com/hits/internal/tally`; the pattern matched the frames above it.

choices.text: The option rounds small functions down to zero
choices.why: That is closer to `-nodefraction`, and it hides rows rather than changing any percentage.

choices.text: The runtime was charged to `Count`'s callers instead
choices.why: That is `-hide`, which keeps the samples and moves their time to the caller.

prompt: Match each `go tool pprof` option with what it does to a report.
hint: Two of them are easy to confuse, and one description fits none.

pairs.right: keeps only samples whose stack contains a match
removes matching frames, charging their time to the caller
drops every sample whose stack contains a match
hides rows whose cum is under 5% of the total

right_distractors: counts how many times each function was called

prompt: You suspect `time.Parse` and are about to write your own timestamp parser. `-list tally.Parse` shows line 31, the `time.Parse` call, at 670 ms and line 27, `strings.Fields`, at 2.53 s. What does the listing tell you about your plan?
hint: Compare the two lines before choosing which to rewrite.

choices.text: Go ahead: dates are always the slow part of a log parser
choices.why: The listing measures this parser, and here the timestamp is about a quarter of the splitting.

choices.text: Rewrite both, since together they are over 3 seconds
choices.why: Each change is paid for separately; the one on line 27 buys nearly four times as much as the one on line 31.

choices.text: Start with line 27; the timestamp costs a quarter as much
choices.why: Right. The profile ruled out the plan before it cost an afternoon; the timestamp already takes a path written for RFC 3339.

choices.text: The listing cannot compare lines, only functions
choices.why: Comparing lines is exactly what `-list` is for: flat and cum per line.

prompt: In a flame graph, what does the width of a box show?
hint: `tally.Count`'s box spans 82.5% of the picture.

choices.text: When in the run the function was running
choices.why: Left to right is not time; the order of siblings is a drawing choice and means nothing.

choices.text: How many times the function was called
choices.why: A flame graph is drawn from samples; like the table, it has no call counts.

choices.text: The function's flat time
choices.why: Flat is the top edge that nothing covers. Width includes the children above.

choices.text: Its cum: the samples that passed through it
choices.why: Right. A box is as wide as the number of stacks it appears on.

prompt: In the flame graph of section 04, `tally.Count` is very wide and almost entirely covered by boxes above it. What does that shape say?
hint: Width and the bare top edge answer different questions.

choices.text: The boxes above hide some of `Count`'s time from the profile
choices.why: Covering is not hiding: the boxes above are where `Count`'s cum was spent.

choices.text: Count delegates: a big cum, a thin flat
choices.why: Right. Its time is spent in the functions above it, which is the shape of the 0.22 s flat against 4.95 s cum in the table.

choices.text: `Count` is called more often than anything else
choices.why: Nothing in a flame graph counts calls; `Count` ran 200 times and `Parse` 20 million.

choices.text: `Count` is the hot spot to rewrite first
choices.why: Its own code is thin; rewriting its loop buys at most its flat.

prompt: This is the flame graph of the `hits` benchmark, root at the bottom. Put each label on the box it describes.
hint: Width is cum; a bare top edge is flat. Look for the names in the boxes.

labels.text: the widest bare top edge: the most flat time
the call in package tally that costs most in total
each line being copied out of the scanner's buffer

prompt: `go tool pprof -http=localhost:8080 cpu.out` draws its flame graph with the root at the top and the callees hanging below. Reading it, where is a function's flat time?
hint: Turn section 04's rules upside down.

choices.text: The bare lower edge, where no callee hangs
choices.why: Right. The picture is the same, inverted: the part of a box with no child under it is where samples ended.

choices.text: In the box's colour, which marks the hot functions
choices.why: Colour means nothing in a flame graph, in either orientation.

choices.text: Nowhere: an inverted graph shows only cum
choices.why: Turning the picture over changes no number; the bare edge is still there, on the other side.

choices.text: At the top edge of its box, as in section 04
choices.why: Upside down, the box's children are below it, so the bare edge is the bottom one.

prompt: When `split5` declines a line, what does the new `Parse` do?
hint: Read the `if !ok` block.

choices.text: Retries `split5` with the tabs replaced by spaces
choices.why: No rewriting happens; the line goes to `strings.Fields` as it is.

choices.text: Returns an error saying the line is not plain
choices.why: Declining is not an error; plenty of valid lines, with tabs or accents, are not the plain case.

choices.text: Falls back to `strings.Fields`, the old code
choices.why: Right. The old path runs unchanged, so an odd line gets exactly the answer, or the error, it got before.

choices.text: Skips the line and goes on to the next one
choices.why: `Parse` handles one line and returns; nothing in it skips.

prompt: Why does `split5` decline any byte outside `!` to `~`, and not only the tab?
hint: What else does `strings.Fields` split on?

choices.text: `strconv.Atoi` cannot read bytes above `~`
choices.why: `Atoi` only sees the status field, and the check covers the whole line.

choices.text: Because non-ASCII paths are invalid in an access log
choices.why: They are valid, and `Parse` still accepts them; it only sends them down the old path.

choices.text: To make the loop faster, since one comparison is cheaper than two
choices.why: The reason is correctness: the speed comes from not allocating.

choices.text: `strings.Fields` also splits on Unicode spaces
choices.why: Right. Their bytes lie outside printable ASCII; the test broke on exactly those when the check was removed.

prompt: `go test` runs a fuzz target on its seeds every time; to generate new inputs for ten seconds you add `-fuzz FuzzSplit5 -___ 10s`.
hint: The flag that limits how long the fuzzer runs.

prompt: A colleague's version of `split5` returns `ok` for every line with exactly four single spaces and no other checks. All of lesson 5's tests and lesson 1's tests pass. Why is that not enough?
hint: What do those tests feed `Parse`?

choices.text: They pass only because the tests are cached
choices.why: A change to `split5` changes the package, so the go command reruns its tests.

choices.text: Their lines contain no tabs or Unicode spaces, so the bug never runs
choices.why: Right. Tests only find what they feed in; the tricky lines and the fuzz target exist for the inputs nobody wrote a row for.

choices.text: Lesson 5's tests check error messages, not fields
choices.why: They also check a good line's status; the point is that none of their lines is one the colleague's version gets wrong.

choices.text: Passing tests prove nothing until the benchmark also passes
choices.why: A benchmark measures time and fails only on an error; it would not notice wrong fields either.

prompt: Why do both CPU profiles compared with `-diff_base` use `-benchtime 200x` rather than `-benchtime 5s`?
hint: What would two runs of five seconds each contain?

choices.text: Same work in both, so the subtraction compares like with like
choices.why: Right. Five seconds of a faster program is more iterations, and every row would grow just from doing more work.

choices.text: benchstat needs exactly 200 samples per side
choices.why: benchstat reads the `-count 10` result files, not the profiles.

choices.text: `-diff_base` refuses profiles of different durations
choices.why: It subtracts whatever it is given; the trouble is that the result would mean little.

choices.text: 200 iterations are faster to profile than five seconds
choices.why: The old run took about six seconds; speed is not the reason.

prompt: benchstat printed `33.52m ± 7%   18.33m ± 7%  -45.31% (p=0.000 n=10)`. What would it have printed in place of `-45.31%` if the ten new runs had been indistinguishable from the ten old ones?
hint: The symbol benchstat uses for "no significant change".

choices.why: `n` is the number of runs used, ten on each side here.
Two noisy samples almost never have identical medians; benchstat reports the verdict, not a zero.
Right. A tilde means the difference was not significant at the p-value threshold, whatever the medians say.
`±` is the confidence interval of each column, not the verdict on the change.

prompt: Put the steps of section 05 and 06 in the order the lesson did them.
hint: The baseline has to exist before the code changes.
items: record ten runs of the benchmark into `old.txt`
run the tests, then the fuzzer
record ten new runs into `new.txt` and run benchstat

prompt: After the fix, the top row is `split5` at 19.15% flat and the next is 7.04%. Your manager asks for another 30% off the count. What does the profile say about that request?
hint: What is the most that removing the top row entirely could buy?

choices.text: Remove `runtime.asyncPreempt`, which is 7% of pure waste
choices.why: It is the runtime interrupting goroutines; there is no code of `hits` to delete there.

choices.text: Run the benchmark with `-count 20`, which gives a better number
choices.why: More runs narrow the confidence interval; they do not make the code faster.

choices.text: Rewrite `split5` again; it is the top row, so it holds the 30%
choices.why: It holds 19%. Even a free `split5` would not reach 30%.

choices.text: No single change will do; it needs several, or a new design
choices.why: Right. The profile is flat now: the biggest row is under 20%, so 30% means changing the design, such as not copying each line.

prompt: The new memory profile shows 1.02 GB allocated, nearly all of it by `Scanner.Text`. Why is that allocation still there?
hint: What does `Count` pass to `Parse`, and what does a map key need?

choices.text: `split5` failed to remove it because of a bug
choices.why: `split5` removed the slice, the allocation it was written for; `Text` is a different one.

choices.text: `Text` copies each line to make a string
choices.why: Right. Removing it means working on the scanner's bytes and converting only what must outlive the line, a bigger change with its own tests.

choices.text: The garbage collector keeps old lines alive for reuse
choices.why: The live heap was nearly empty in lesson 12; the bytes are allocated and freed, again and again.

choices.text: `-memprofile` counts the benchmark's `os.ReadFile` 200 times
choices.why: The file is read once, before the loop, and it showed as 4.37 MB in lesson 12.
